title: Red fox in cross-stitch
subtitle: A seated fox in rust, white, and black on 14-count Aida
excerpt: A seated red fox is a 70-by-80 stitch piece on 14-count Aida using nine colours to capture the rust coat, white bib, black legs, and distinctive pointed face. The piece finishes at about 13 x 14 cm in a 15 cm hoop and includes a back-stitch whisker layer added after the full crosses.
sourceNotes: Original design for Homemade cross-stitch library. Fox colouring conventions follow natural history illustration tradition.

content.text: Find the centre of the fabric. The centre of the chart falls on the main body of the fox (the large rust block in the torso area). Begin there with DMC 920 (dark rust).
Work the rust coat first (920, 922, 3826) from the body outward, then the pale bib (3024, blanc), the dark legs and tail tip (310, 3371), and finally the face details.
Work the three-quarter stitches at the bib boundary and ear edges in the relevant rust and white colours before adding the back-stitch outline.
Add the back-stitch layer last: the eye outline and pupil in 3371, the whisker lines in three single strands of 3865 (off-white), each whisker one long stitch from muzzle to tip.
Wash gently in cool water, press face-down, and allow to dry flat. Display in the hoop on a wall or frame under glass. The rust palette suits a wooden frame with a white mount.

A similar approach works for any medium-sized woodland animal with a clear palette. The owl project in this sub-category uses the same technique with a different shape and a warm brown-and-cream palette.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.
